finalText:
**Merge** combines two branches and keeps both timelines intact. Git creates a commit that says "these branches came together here." Your history shows the work happened in parallel. It's safe, it's honest, and it never rewrites anything.

**Rebase** takes your commits and replays them on top of the other branch, like you wrote them there all along. Your history becomes a straight line. It's cleaner to read, but it rewrites your commits, so you can't do it on branches other people are using.

Reach for **merge** when the branch is shared or pushed. Use it on main, or when a teammate is working on the same branch. The safety matters more than the pretty history.

Reach for **rebase** on your own local branches, right before you merge to main. It cleans up your commits so the final merge is simple. It's also nice during a longer feature branch to stay in sync with main without accumulating merge commits. Just don't rebase anything you've already pushed or shared.

The one hard rule: once you push a branch, don't rebase it. The commits change, and anyone pulling your branch gets confused.
